faqs.answer: 15 g of coffee to 250 g of water for one cup, at 1:16.7. That is the 60 g per litre recipe, and it scales: 30 g for two cups, 60 g for a litre.
faqs.question: How much coffee for a V60?

faqs.answer: Because the standard V60 recipe is 60 g of coffee per litre of water, and 1,000 divided by 60 is 16.7. It is James Hoffmann's recipe, and it has become the V60 default. 1:16 is close enough that either works.
faqs.question: Why 1:16.7 and not 1:16?

faqs.answer: Medium-fine, like coarse sand. Too fine and the drawdown stalls. Too coarse and the water runs through before the flavour comes out.
faqs.question: What grind should I use for a V60?

faqs.answer: About three minutes from the first pour to the last drip, including a 30-second bloom. Faster than two and a half minutes usually means the grind is too coarse.
faqs.question: How long should a V60 brew take?

faqs.answer: It helps, because a slow, controlled pour is the whole technique. A small jug with a steady hand works too. The scale matters more than the kettle.
faqs.question: Do I need a gooseneck kettle for a V60?

felicityNote: The V60 is my fussy-morning brewer. Fifteen grams, 250 grams of water, three minutes, and it tastes like the coffee shop down the road.

formula.text: Water = coffee × 16.7. Coffee = water ÷ 16.7. Or 60 g of coffee per litre of water.

howToSteps.name: Rinse the filter
howToSteps.text: Set the V60 on your mug or server, put the paper filter in, and rinse it with hot water. Tip the rinse water away.

howToSteps.name: Add the coffee
howToSteps.text: Put 15 g of medium-fine coffee in the filter for one cup, or 30 g for two. Level the bed with a gentle shake.

howToSteps.name: Bloom for 30 seconds
howToSteps.text: Pour twice the coffee weight in water at 92 to 96 C and wait 30 seconds while the grounds swell and release gas.

howToSteps.name: Pour in stages
howToSteps.text: Pour the rest of the water in slow circles, in two or three stages. The brew should finish in about three minutes.

title: Hario V60 Coffee to Water Ratio
tutorial: The V60 has its own ratio, and it comes from one recipe: James Hoffmann's ultimate V60, 60 g of coffee per litre of water. That works out to 1:16.7, which is 15 g of coffee for a 250 ml cup. It is the closest thing the V60 has to a standard.

The cone and the large single hole make the V60 drain fast, so the drawdown responds directly to the dose and the grind. A ratio change shows up in the cup straight away. The working range is 1:15 to 1:17, and 1:16 is a fine starting point if you prefer round numbers, but 1:16.7 is the recipe most V60 brewers actually use.

Grind medium-fine and keep the brew to about three minutes. The V60 rewards a steady, slow pour in circles, and it punishes a fast one: dump the water in and the bed floods, the brew stalls, and the cup tastes bitter. A gooseneck kettle makes the pour easy, but a steady hand and a small jug work too.

The bloom matters more here than in a Chemex because the bed is thinner. Pour twice the coffee weight in water, wait 30 seconds, and watch the grounds swell. Then pour the rest in two or three stages, letting the water drain a little between pours.

Weigh everything, every time. A tablespoon of ground coffee weighs about 5 grams, but it varies with the roast and the grind, and at 1:16.7 a few grams either way is the difference between a clean cup and a thin one. The scale is the cheapest upgrade a V60 brewer can buy.
